From the early 1930s until 1969, Cadillac was once a household name in Australia. Luxury buyers could sample several of its models made their way Down Under, including the classic Eldorado. After that, the brand disappeared from local shores.

Speaking to a crowd at the Australian launch of Cadillac's new Formula 1 team in Melbourne back in March, which I attended, GM president Mark Reuss said the automaker had come close to relaunching Cadillac in Australia in the early 2000s, but the plan ultimately fell through. In the late 2010s, I even spotted several camouflaged prototypes testing , as the brand again toyed with the idea of returning. Now, Cadillac is officially back, albeit as an EV-only brand.

Not long before the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety was informing drivers of how dangerous or safe a car was , James S. Kemper was on a mission to improve road safety. Kemper worked in the insurance world in his first job out of high school. He was an "office boy" for Central Mutual Insurance according to his New York Times obituary , but he went on to produce his own driver safety materials: educational films.

The films were made by Kemper's personal insurance company, Lumbermen Mutual Casualty, and in partnership with the LAPD and Traffic Safety Films Inc. The LAPD connection helped bring "Sergeant Bruce" to the films, who starred on-camera several times as the presenter of important safety lessons — each video with its own specific theme. After a Missouri town voted unanimously to cancel its contract with Flock in October, the town, like many others who have recently cancelled contracts, went ahead and covered its flock cameras in black trash bags . Not two weeks later, the town's police department found not only were the cameras still on, but they continued to record vehicles, using infrared technology for the dark trash-bag induced conditions.

Excelsior Springs Police Department took to Facebook on November 5 to inform its residents of the issue. The department's Lieutenant Ryan Dowdy told Local 12 that the city initially placed bags over the cameras when they voted to end its contract with Flock and remove the cameras. However, not only are the cameras still on, the black garbage bags do not seem to block Flock's automated license plate reader's infrared technology. The company touts that tech on its own website as "nighttime performance that doesn't quit."

New EV sales in the U.S. are also struggling, and automakers are struggling to find buyers. The good news is, I have an actual, viable solution that automakers are free steal borrow.

OK, so we've seen that spending time living with an EV , even temporarily, goes a long way to debunking pro-oil propaganda and can change people's minds about whether or not an EV is right for them. Personally, I think the easiest way to make that happen is for owners who want to see EVs get more popular to lend their cars to as many people as they can, for at least 3 days at a time. Ideally, automakers would offer 120-hour test drives to anyone who wants one, but that would be wildly expensive, so I understand why it's hard to even get a 72-hour loan.

Lincoln has been selling the second-generation Aviator in the U.S. since 2019 . It received a thorough facelift for the 2025 model year, but is starting to feel its age. While the brand appears to have forgotten about America's Aviator, Lincoln has worked with Chinese joint venture partner Changan to develop a new Aviator plug-in hybrid that might leave North American buyers feeling a little envious. This new model is officially known as the Aviator EX8 and it shares some obvious design similarities with the American SUV, though it is a completely different vehicle.

The front-end includes a familiar Lincoln grille, relatively simple and stylish LED headlights, and upright air vents towards the base of the bumper. America's Lincoln Aviator remains one of the best-looking SUVs on the market — at least in our eyes — and features lovely, flowing lines that aren't often seen in this segment. Not to be confused with the Chinese Lincoln Corsair , it sits slightly taller and has a more upright design, which is immediately apparent when looking at the side profile with its flatter roof and angular windows. The new shape isn't necessarily a bad thing, it's just different.

Honda is already well entrenched in Ohio. The Japanese automaker has two vehicle assembly factories in the state, in East Liberty and Marysville, along with the Anna Engine Plant and a transmission facility in Russells Point. Now Honda is taking its commitment to Ohio even further, announcing today a plant to build a new factory in Central Ohio and to invest $3 billion into the project.

The new factory will be located near Honda’s existing manufacturing facilities, on land between the East Liberty and Marysville plants. Production is set to kick off in 2029, and the factory will have a planned capacity of 240,000 vehicles, boosting Honda’s U.S. production capacity to around 1.3 million vehicles per year. The new factory will create over 2000 new jobs, Honda says. Honda didn’t specify what would be built at the new factory but did say it would be capable of producing everything from gas-powered models to hybrids and full EVs.

The weekend at Interlagos broke the recent trend of rain halting on-track action instead of shaking up the competitive order. Actually racing in the rain had become as rare as spotting a dodo bird in the wild.

On one level, the comparison between the Mach-E and the Fathom EV battery is apples-to-oranges. The 2021 Mach-E deployed [correction: NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) batteries with Standard Range at 68 kWh usable capacity as launched, and Extended Range at 88 kWh usable capacity as launched]. Ford is equipping the Fathom with an LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) EV battery. LFP is a relatively new, more economical formula than Li-ion. All else being equal the tradeoff is lower range, though some Ford watchers point out that drivers can order their Fathom with an optional extended-range battery.

Car safety has come a long way since the days of yore. Ask the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS). The organization's crash testing standards have evolved significantly over 30+ years as more new vehicles keep getting better at protecting their occupants. By now, we're pretty familiar with the IIHS Top Safety Pick awards. However, just because your second-gen 2011 Hyundai Tucson has the Top Safety Pick under its belt doesn't mean it's as safe as the third-gen 2021 model, which also happens to be a Top Safety Pick winner.

Although the IIHS rates the small SUV highly , understand that it also keeps updating the award's eligibility criteria as the years go by. For example, headlights were not even part of the Top Safety Pick criteria in 2010, nor were vehicle-to-vehicle or pedestrian crash-prevention features. And Top Safety Pick+ wasn't even a thing before 2013. In fact, looking at the many generations of the small SUV, it's fair to conclude that fourth-generation Tucsons (2022-2026) appear to be the safest, according to the IIHS. Not only have certain fourth-generation Tucsons gone through the organization's slew of updated testing standards, but they have consistently been part of the IIHS Top Safety Pick+ category between 2022 and 2026, unlike the third or prior generation models.
